youtube.title: Jocelyn Bell Burnell: She Found the Signal, He Got the Nobel
youtube.description:
Jocelyn Bell Burnell was a 24-year-old Cambridge student in 1967 when she found a radio signal pulsing every 1.3 seconds, so regular that her team nicknamed it LGM-1, for Little Green Men.

Then she found a second one in another part of the sky, and the answer turned out to be a spinning neutron star: PSR B1919+21, the first pulsar ever discovered. The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to her supervisor Antony Hewish and to Martin Ryle. In 2018 she won the $3 million Special Breakthrough Prize and gave all of it to fund physics PhD students from under-represented groups. Astronomers are still finding radio sources nobody can explain, like VT J1906+0849, which has been glowing for about twenty years.

Subscribe to Stickstory for a strange true story every day. Should she have shared that Nobel Prize? Tell me in the comments!

scenes.text: Her signal was nicknamed Little Green Men.
scenes.visual: A chart-recorder paper strip runs from the middle of the frame into a recorder box at the right; the paper scrolls and the pen draws a noisy trace with a sharp spike every 1.3 seconds (the newest spike flashes red). On 'Little' a little green ink alien doodle with antennae pops up on top of the strip and waves; on 'Men' a red 'LGM-1' stamp slams in at the upper right; the big fez narrator at the left points at the strip, then jumps back in shock.

scenes.text: Astronomers still find signals they can't explain.
scenes.visual: Night sky with ink stars; a slowly turning spiral galaxy at the upper left sends ink wave fronts across the sky into the feed of a big radio telescope dish on a hill; the feed glows gold as each wave arrives; on 'explain' a huge red question mark pops over the dish; the fez narrator at the lower left watches through binoculars, then shrugs.

scenes.text: But the first big one hit a student's desk in 1967.
scenes.visual: Inside a 1960s observatory hut: a night window at the upper left (hatched dark sky, twinkling stars, a crescent moon), a wooden desk with a chart-recorder box (dial, red lamp) spilling paper over the desk edge into a pile of folds on the floor; on 'hit' a red zig-zag signal shoots from the window into the recorder with a gold spark, the frame jolts and the dial needle swings; a big '1967' sits at the upper right; Jocelyn Bell (hatless stick figure with a dark bob) stands at the left thinking, then jumps in surprise; the fez narrator at the right points at the recorder.

scenes.text: Jocelyn Bell, 24, saw it pulse every 1.3 seconds.
scenes.visual: Close on the chart paper strip high in the frame: the pen keeps drawing a spike exactly every 1.3 seconds (1.337 s), in time with the real signal; on '1.3' a red bracket spans the two newest spikes and a big red '1.3 s' punches in above it; below, Jocelyn Bell (dark bob) points up at the spikes, and the fez narrator at the right looks through binoculars, then points.

scenes.text: Aliens, right? Then she found another, across the sky.
scenes.visual: A round hand-drawn star chart (grid circles, constellation lines, ink stars) slowly turning; source A on the left pulses gold rings with a red core and a red handwritten 'ALIENS?' next to it; on 'another' a second pulsing source pops up on the far right side of the chart and a red dashed arc draws from one to the other; on 'across' 'ALIENS?' is struck through in red; the fez narrator at the lower right looks through binoculars, then shrugs.

scenes.text: It was a spinning dead star: the first pulsar.
scenes.visual: A small dense hatched neutron star with dipole field loops and a red spin arrow; two gold lighthouse beams sweep round once every 1.3 seconds and an ink Earth with continents at the right flashes red each time beam A crosses it; on 'dead' a handwritten 'dead star' appears, on 'pulsar' a red 'PULSAR' box slams in; the fez narrator at the lower left points at the star, then jumps back in shock.

scenes.text: Guess who got the Nobel Prize? Her supervisor.
scenes.visual: A big gold medal stamped '1974' swings on a red ribbon in the middle of the frame with gold glints; Jocelyn Bell stands at the left beside a low stage; on 'supervisor' the medal arcs over and lands round the neck of her supervisor (hatless man on the stage), who waves happily, while Jocelyn shrugs, worried; the fez narrator at the right shrugs, angry.

scenes.text: In 2018 she won three million dollars,
scenes.visual: A big Fraunces money counter at the top runs from $0 up to $3,000,000 on 'three' with a gold underline, while green ink banknotes rain down; under it a handwritten 'Breakthrough Prize'; Jocelyn Bell, now with grey hair, stands at the left and waves; the fez narrator at the right jumps back in shock.

scenes.text: and gave it all to students like her.
scenes.visual: Banknotes fly in arcs from grey-haired Jocelyn Bell at the left into the hands of three young physics students at the right while the money counter at the top runs down to a red $0; a red box 'ALL OF IT' slams in on 'students' and the students wave.

scenes.text: Subscribe for a true story like this every day.
scenes.visual: The pulsar again, smaller at the upper left, its gold beams still sweeping round every 1.3 seconds; a handwritten 'still ticking' next to it; the fez narrator in the middle waves at the viewer, then points up at the star.
